tips.title: Three fossils, three dates
tips.body: **Ardi 4.4 · Lucy 3.2 · Leakey 1.6 million years ago.** The specification names these three with their dates, so learn them as a set — and note they run **oldest to most recent**, which is what makes them evidence.

tips.title: Penta means five
tips.body: A **pentadactyl limb** is built on a **five-digit plan**. The same plan appears in a human arm, a bat wing, a whale flipper and a horse leg, even where digits have since been reduced, as in the horse — very different jobs, one underlying structure.

tips.title: A shared plan means a shared ancestor
tips.body: If limbs doing **completely different jobs** share the **same bone arrangement**, the simplest explanation is that they were **inherited from a common ancestor** and then modified. A designer starting fresh each time would not reuse an unsuitable plan.

tips.title: Three domains replaced five kingdoms
tips.body: The change came from **genetic analysis** — comparing DNA and RNA rather than appearance. It showed that organisms that **look similar** can be **very distantly related**, which classification by appearance had missed entirely.

tips.title: Stone tools are dated from their environment
tips.body: Tools themselves carry no date. They are dated **from the rock layers and materials around them** — so the tools show **how technology developed over time** once that dating is in place.

why.matters:
Evolution cannot be watched from start to finish, so the case for it is built the way a case is built in a court: many independent kinds of evidence that only make sense together.

Fossils give a sequence in time. Anatomy gives the same bones rearranged for different jobs. And DNA, which nobody had when the theory was proposed, agrees with both — which is the strongest thing that can happen to an idea: a new kind of evidence that could have refuted it and did not.

examples.title: Why three fossils are worth more than one
examples.body:
The specification names **Ardi** at 4.4 million years, **Lucy** at 3.2, and the **Leakey** fossil at 1.6 — a span of about **2.8 million years**.

One skeleton would be a curiosity. Three, at known and different ages, make a **sequence**: brain size and the way of walking change steadily from one to the next, in the direction the theory predicts. That is the point about evidence — no single find proves anything, and a trend across several is hard to explain any other way.

props.caption: How long ago each lived, in millions of years

visual.alt: Three bars in proportion showing when each named fossil lived: Ardi at four point four million years ago, Lucy at three point two and the Leakey fossil at one point six

examples.title: Why a bat, a whale and you have the same bones
examples.body:
A bat's wing, a whale's flipper, a horse's leg and your arm do entirely different jobs, and all four are built from the **same set of bones** in the same arrangement — one, then two, then a group of small ones, then five digits, even where some digits have since been reduced, as in the horse.

If each had been designed for its job there would be no reason for that. If they are modified versions of the limb of a **common ancestor** there is no other possibility. The pentadactyl limb is evidence precisely because it is inconvenient: nobody would build a flipper this way from scratch.

visual.alt: A table of four animals whose limbs do completely different jobs — flying, swimming, running and gripping — and which are all built on the same five-digit pentadactyl plan

examples.title: Why biologists threw away the five kingdoms
examples.body:
Classification used to be built on what organisms **look like**, which is the only evidence anybody had. It put things together that looked alike and it was right often enough to be useful.

Then genetic analysis arrived and showed that some organisms grouped together were no more related than a plant and an animal. The **three domains** — archaea, bacteria and eukaryota — follow the DNA instead, and two groups that both look like ordinary bacteria turned out to be the deepest split in life. The system changed because the evidence changed, which is how it is supposed to work.

visual.alt: A table contrasting the five kingdoms, built on what organisms look like, with the three domains, built on genetic analysis, which split what had been a single group of bacteria into two separate domains

steps.title: Fossil evidence for human evolution
steps.body:
**The specification names three specific fossil finds with their dates**, and expects you to know them.

**Ardi, from 4.4 million years ago.** The oldest of the three. Its feet were still suited to **climbing**, with a big toe that could grasp like a thumb, but other features suggest it could also **walk upright**. It sits close to the point where our line diverged from other apes.

**Lucy, from 3.2 million years ago.** More clearly adapted to **walking upright** than Ardi — the structure of the knee and pelvis shows a more human style of walking — though the brain was still small and the arms long.

**Richard Leakey's discovery of fossils from 1.6 million years ago.** More **human-like** again: a larger brain, a shorter face, and a body better suited to walking and running long distances.

**What makes this a sequence rather than three curiosities.** Laid out by date the fossils span **2.8 million years**, and across that span the features become **progressively more human**: upright walking develops first, and the **brain enlarges later**.

**That order is itself the evidence.** A gradual change in the same direction over millions of years is what evolution predicts. If the fossils showed modern features appearing suddenly, or in no particular order, the theory would be in difficulty.

**Why fossils are still an incomplete record.** Fossilisation is **rare** — it needs particular conditions, and soft tissue almost never survives. Many fossils have been **destroyed** by geological activity, and many remain **undiscovered**. So the record has gaps, which is why each new find matters so much.

steps.title: Stone tools
steps.body:
**The specification asks for the evidence for human evolution based on stone tools**, in two parts: **the development of stone tools over time**, and **how these can be dated from their environment**.

**How tools developed.** The earliest stone tools are **simple**: a pebble struck to give a sharp edge, used for cutting or scraping. Over time they become steadily more **complex and specialised** — worked on both sides, shaped to a deliberate design, and made for particular purposes such as hand axes, blades, spear points and arrowheads.

**Why that development is evidence.** Making a more complex tool requires **planning**, **manual skill**, and the ability to **teach the technique to others**. A trend towards more sophisticated tools therefore tracks **increasing brain size and intelligence** — and it can be set against the fossil record, which shows the brain enlarging over the same period.

**How the tools are dated.** This is the part the specification asks for explicitly, and it is the part students omit. **Stone tools themselves cannot be dated directly** — stone carries no clock, and the rock a tool is made from is far older than the tool.

Instead they are dated **from their environment**: from the **rock layers (strata)** in which they are found, and from other **materials found alongside them**. Layers of **volcanic ash** above and below a tool can be dated from the radioactive elements they contain, which gives the tool an age range.

**Deeper layers are older**, so a tool found in a deeper layer is older than one above it. That gives at least a **relative** order even where an exact date cannot be fixed.

**So the argument runs: date the layers, place the tools in them, and the development of tool-making over time becomes visible.**

steps.title: The pentadactyl limb
steps.body:
*(Biology only.)* **The specification asks how the anatomy of the pentadactyl limb provides scientists with evidence for evolution.**

**What it is.** *Penta* means **five** and *dactyl* means **digit**, so a **pentadactyl limb** is a limb built on the **five-digit plan**: one bone in the upper part, two in the lower, then a group of small bones, then five digits. In some species the digits have since been reduced or lost: a **horse** stands on a single digit, and a **bird's wing** has three. The underlying plan is still the same.

**Where it is found.** In a **human arm**, a **bat's wing**, a **whale's flipper**, a **horse's leg** and a **bird's wing**. These limbs do **completely different jobs** — grasping, flying, swimming, running — and yet all are built on the **same underlying plan**, with the same bones in the same relative positions, differing only in their **size and proportions**.

**Why this is evidence for evolution.** If each species had arisen **independently**, there would be no reason for a swimming limb and a flying limb to share a bone arrangement. A structure designed from scratch for swimming would look nothing like one designed for flight.

**The simplest explanation is common ancestry.** The species **inherited the same limb structure from a shared ancestor**, and natural selection then **modified** it for each different way of life — lengthening some bones, fusing or reducing others — without ever starting again.

**That is the key idea: evolution modifies what is already there.** It cannot redesign from nothing, because each generation must be viable. So an inherited plan persists even when it is not the arrangement anyone would choose for the job — and that persistence is exactly what makes it evidence.

**What the limb does not tell you** is how closely two species are related. Limb shape also depends on what the limb is used for, so a bat's wing can look more like a bird's wing than like a whale's flipper. Comparing **DNA sequences** is the measure of relatedness.

steps.title: From five kingdoms to three domains
steps.body:
**The specification asks how genetic analysis has led to the suggestion of the three domains rather than the five kingdoms classification method.**

**The five kingdoms system** classified all living things into **5** groups — animals, plants, fungi, protists and prokaryotes — largely on the basis of **observable features**: what organisms looked like, how they were built and how they fed.

**The problem with classifying by appearance.** Organisms that **look alike** are not always closely related. Similar conditions can produce similar features in **unrelated** species, so appearance can be misleading — and microorganisms in particular offer very few visible features to compare at all.

**What genetic analysis changed.** Comparing **DNA and RNA sequences** gives a far more direct measure of relatedness: the more similar the sequences, the more recently the species shared a common ancestor. This can be done for **any** organism, including bacteria, where appearance gives almost nothing to work with.

**What it revealed.** The organisms that had all been lumped together as "prokaryotes" turned out to include **two groups so genetically different** that each was given its own domain. **Archaea** turned out to be more closely related to **eukaryotes**, including us, than to **bacteria**. Grouping them together had hidden one of the deepest divisions in the living world.

**The three domains system** therefore divides life into **3**: **archaea**, **bacteria** and **eukaryota** (organisms whose cells have a nucleus — animals, plants, fungi and protists together).

**Notice what this is an example of.** New **evidence** — genetic sequencing — led to an established **classification being revised**, exactly as new evidence revised the model of the atom. The five kingdoms system was not careless; it used the best evidence available at the time, which was **appearance**.

steps.title: Going deeper
steps.body:
**Learn the three fossils with their dates.** **Ardi (4.4 Mya), Lucy (3.2 Mya), Leakey (1.6 Mya)**. The specification names them explicitly, so they are straightforward recall — and quoting a date lifts an answer immediately.

**Explain the fossils as a sequence, not a list.** What matters is that across **2.8 million years** the features become **progressively more human**, and in a particular order — **upright walking first, larger brains later**. A gradual directional change is what evolution predicts; three unconnected facts are not evidence of anything.

**Acknowledge the gaps in the fossil record.** Fossilisation is **rare**, soft tissue rarely survives, many fossils have been **destroyed** and many are **undiscovered**. Saying so is not weakening your answer — it shows you understand what the evidence can and cannot support.

**Do not forget how stone tools are dated.** They **cannot be dated directly**; they are dated **from their environment** — the **rock layers** and other **materials** found with them. This is asked for specifically and is regularly left out.

*(Biology only.)* **Make the pentadactyl argument properly.** It is not simply that limbs are similar. It is that limbs doing **completely different jobs** share the **same bone plan**, which independent origins would not predict. The explanation is that the plan was **inherited from a common ancestor** and then **modified** — because evolution can only **change what is already there**, never start again.

**Explain the domains change through the weakness it fixed.** Five kingdoms classified by **appearance**, and appearance can mislead: look-alikes may be unrelated, and microorganisms offer little to compare. **Genetic analysis** compares **DNA and RNA** directly, and revealed that the "prokaryotes" contained **two profoundly different groups** — a division appearance had entirely concealed.

**Frame both classification and the atom as the same story.** New **evidence** revises an established **model**. The five kingdoms system was not careless — it used the best evidence then available. That observation is worth making explicitly when a question asks why classification changed.

**Say that greater similarity in DNA sequences means a more recent common ancestor.** That is what turns a similarity into a statement about **relatedness**. It does not apply to how alike limbs look, because limb shape also follows what the limb is used for.

steps.body:
- Three named fossils: **Ardi — 4.4 Mya**, **Lucy — 3.2 Mya**, **Leakey — 1.6 Mya**.
- They span **2.8 million years**, with features becoming **progressively more human**.
- **Upright walking develops first**; the **brain enlarges later**.
- The fossil record has **gaps**: fossilisation is rare, and many fossils are destroyed or undiscovered.
- **Stone tools** become more **complex and specialised** over time.
- More complex tools require **planning, skill and teaching** — tracking increasing intelligence.
- Tools are **dated from their environment** — the **rock layers** and nearby materials — not directly.
- A **pentadactyl limb** is built on a shared **five-digit** bone plan, even where digits are reduced.
- It is found in the **human arm, bat wing, whale flipper and horse leg**.
- Different **jobs**, same **plan** — best explained by a **common ancestor**.
- Evolution **modifies what already exists** rather than redesigning.
- **Five kingdoms** classified by **observable features**.
- Appearance can mislead: look-alikes may be **unrelated**.
- **Genetic analysis** of **DNA and RNA** measures relatedness directly.
- It revealed deep divisions among prokaryotes, giving the **3 domains**: **archaea, bacteria, eukaryota**.

questions.prompt: Describe the evidence for human evolution from fossils and from stone tools, and explain the limitations of this evidence.
questions.solution:
**Fossil evidence.** The specification names three finds, and their **dates** are what make them a sequence rather than three isolated discoveries.

**Ardi**, from **4.4 million years ago**, is the oldest. Its feet were still suited to **climbing**, with a grasping big toe, but other features suggest it could also **walk upright**.

**Lucy**, from **3.2 million years ago**, is more clearly adapted to **walking upright** — the structure of the pelvis and knee indicates a more human style of walking — although the brain was still small and the arms long.

**Richard Leakey's fossils**, from **1.6 million years ago**, are more human-like again, with a **larger brain**, a shorter face and a body suited to walking and running long distances.

**What the sequence shows.** Across these **2.8 million years** the features become **progressively more human**, and in a particular **order**: **upright walking develops first, and brain size increases later**. A gradual, directional change over a long period is exactly what evolution predicts. Had modern features appeared suddenly, or in no particular order, the theory would be in difficulty.

**Stone tool evidence.** The earliest stone tools are **simple** — a pebble struck to give a sharp edge for cutting or scraping. Over time they become steadily more **complex and specialised**: worked on both sides, deliberately shaped, and made for particular purposes such as hand axes, blades and spear points.

This is evidence because making a more complex tool demands **planning**, **manual skill** and the ability to **teach the technique to others**. The trend therefore tracks **increasing brain size and intelligence**, and it can be set alongside the fossil record, which shows the brain enlarging over the same period.

**How the tools are dated** is an essential part of the argument. Stone tools **cannot be dated directly**, because the stone itself formed long before anyone shaped it — dating it would give the age of the rock, not the tool. Instead they are dated **from their environment**: from the **rock layers (strata)** in which they are found, and from other **materials** alongside them, such as layers of volcanic ash above and below them, whose age can be measured from the radioactive elements they contain. Since **deeper layers are older**, this gives at least a **relative** order of tools even where an exact date is not possible.

**Limitations.** The **fossil record is incomplete**. Fossilisation requires particular conditions and is **rare**; **soft tissue** almost never survives, so much about these species is unknown; many fossils have been **destroyed** by geological activity; and many remain **undiscovered**. This means there are genuine gaps in the sequence.

Stone tools have their own limitation: they show what was **made**, but tools of wood, bone or plant material rarely survive, so the picture is biased towards stone.

Acknowledging this does not undermine the case. The argument does not rest on any single fossil but on the **pattern** the evidence forms — and each new find is a further test of it, which is why individual discoveries matter so much.

**Stone tool evidence.** The earliest stone tools are **simple** — a pebble struck to give a sharp edge for cutting or scraping. Over time they become steadily more **complex and specialised**: worked on both sides, deliberately shaped, and made for particular purposes such as hand axes, blades and spear points.

This is evidence because making a more complex tool demands **planning**, **manual skill** and the ability to **teach the technique to others**. The trend therefore tracks **increasing brain size and intelligence**, and it can be set alongside the fossil record, which shows the brain enlarging over the same period.

**How the tools are dated** is an essential part of the argument. Stone tools **cannot be dated directly**, because the stone itself formed long before anyone shaped it — dating it would give the age of the rock, not the tool. Instead they are dated **from their environment**: from the **rock layers (strata)** in which they are found, and from other **materials** alongside them, such as layers of volcanic ash above and below them, whose age can be measured from the radioactive elements they contain. Since **deeper layers are older**, this gives at least a **relative** order of tools even where an exact date is not possible.

**Limitations.** The **fossil record is incomplete**. Fossilisation requires particular conditions and is **rare**; **soft tissue** almost never survives, so much about these species is unknown; many fossils have been **destroyed** by geological activity; and many remain **undiscovered**. This means there are genuine gaps in the sequence.

Stone tools have their own limitation: they show what was **made**, but tools of wood, bone or plant material rarely survive, so the picture is biased towards stone.

Acknowledging this does not undermine the case. The argument does not rest on any single fossil but on the **pattern** the evidence forms — and each new find is a further test of it, which is why individual discoveries matter so much.

questions.prompt: Explain how the pentadactyl limb and genetic analysis each provide evidence about how organisms are related.
questions.solution:
**The pentadactyl limb.** *Penta* means five and *dactyl* means digit, so a pentadactyl limb is one built on a **five-digit plan**, with a characteristic arrangement: one bone in the upper limb, two in the lower, a group of small bones, then the five digits.

The same plan is found in a **human arm**, a **bat's wing**, a **whale's flipper**, a **horse's leg** and a **bird's wing**. What is striking is that these limbs do **completely different jobs** — grasping, flying, swimming, running — and yet share the same bones in the same relative positions, differing only in **size and proportion**. A bat's digits are enormously elongated to support a wing membrane; a horse's are mostly reduced or lost; a bird's wing keeps only three; a whale's are shortened and broadened.

**Why this is evidence for a common ancestor.** If each species had arisen **independently**, there would be **no reason** for a swimming limb and a flying limb to share a bone arrangement. Structures designed from scratch for those two tasks would look nothing alike — one would be a paddle and the other a membrane frame, with no expectation of matching bones.

The simplest explanation is that the species **inherited the same limb structure from a shared ancestor**, and that natural selection then **modified** it for each way of life.

This points to something fundamental about how evolution works: **it modifies what is already there rather than redesigning from nothing**, because every generation must be viable. So an inherited plan persists even where it is not the arrangement anyone would choose for the job — and that persistence is precisely what makes it evidence. Limb shape also follows what the limb is used for, so how alike two limbs look is not a measure of how closely the species are related.

**Genetic analysis** provides the same kind of evidence far more directly. Comparing **DNA and RNA sequences** measures relatedness itself: the more similar the sequences, the more recently the organisms shared an ancestor.

It also works where anatomy fails. The **five kingdoms** system classified organisms largely by **observable features**, and that has two weaknesses. Organisms in similar conditions can evolve **similar features without being related**, so appearance can mislead. And **microorganisms** offer very few visible features to compare at all.

**What genetic analysis revealed** was that the organisms grouped together as "prokaryotes" on the basis of appearance actually contain **two profoundly different groups** — **archaea** and **bacteria** — which are so genetically distinct that each was given its own domain. Archaea turned out to be **more closely related to eukaryotes**, including us, than to bacteria. Classification by appearance had concealed one of the deepest divisions in the living world.

This led to the **three domains** system — **archaea, bacteria and eukaryota** — replacing the five kingdoms.

**The two kinds of evidence agree**, which is what makes the case strong. Anatomy suggested relatedness through shared structures; genetics confirmed and refined it, and corrected it where appearance had been misleading. And the change itself illustrates how science works: the five kingdoms system was **not careless** — it used the best evidence available at the time — and it was revised when better evidence became possible.

found in limbs used for very different purposes
independent origins would not give the same plan
so it was inherited and then modified
genetic analysis compares DNA and RNA
leading to three domains rather than five kingdoms

questions.prompt:
The table gives rounded estimates of brain volume for the three fossils named in the specification. Estimates vary between studies.

| Fossil | Lived (million years ago) | Brain volume (cm³) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Ardi | 4.4 | 350 |
| Lucy | 3.2 | 450 |
| Leakey's fossil | 1.6 | 900 |

Calculate the mean increase in brain volume per million years between Lucy and Leakey's fossil.
questions.solution: The increase is $900 - 450 = 450$ cm³, over $3.2 - 1.6 = 1.6$ million years. So the mean increase is $450 \div 1.6 = $ **281.25**, about **281 cm³ per million years**. Between Ardi and Lucy the increase was only $450 - 350 = 100$ cm³ over 1.2 million years, which fits the pattern of **upright walking first and brain enlargement later**.

markScheme.description: divides by 1.6 million years
281 (accept 280 to 282)

questions.prompt: Ardi, Lucy and the fossils discovered by Leakey are three fossil finds that provide evidence for human evolution. Which list puts them in order from oldest to youngest?
questions.skill: the order of the fossil finds
questions.solution: **Ardi, then Lucy, then Leakey's fossils.** Ardi lived **4.4 million years ago**, Lucy **3.2 million years ago**, and the fossils Leakey discovered are from **1.6 million years ago**. Read in that order, the fossils become progressively more human: upright walking appears first, and a larger brain later.

markScheme.description: Ardi, Lucy, Leakey's fossils

options: Lucy, then Ardi, then Leakey's fossils
Leakey's fossils, then Lucy, then Ardi
Ardi, then Lucy, then Leakey's fossils

questions.prompt: A horse's leg ends in a single hoofed digit, yet biologists still describe it as a pentadactyl limb. Why?
questions.skill: reduced digits in a pentadactyl limb
questions.solution: **Its bones follow the same plan as other pentadactyl limbs, with fewer digits.** A pentadactyl limb is built on the five-digit plan: one bone in the upper part, two in the lower part (fused together in the horse), a group of small bones, then the digits. What makes a limb pentadactyl is that underlying plan, not the number of digits it ends with. In the horse, one digit carries the hoof and the others have been reduced or lost, in the same way that a bird's wing has three digits. The plan was inherited from an ancestor with five digits and modified by natural selection for running. A hoof is not five bones fused together, a limb is not classed as pentadactyl just because it is used for walking, and a horse does not grasp with its legs.

markScheme.description: the bones follow the same pentadactyl plan, with the digits reduced

options: Its hoof is made of five bones fused together, one from each of its five digits
Its bones follow the same plan as other pentadactyl limbs, with fewer digits
Every limb that an animal uses for walking is classed as a pentadactyl limb
A horse uses its front legs for grasping objects, in the same way as a hand

questions.prompt: At a dig, the layers of rock have not been disturbed since they were laid down. Two layers of volcanic ash have been dated: ash X to 0.9 million years ago and ash Y, lower down, to 1.4 million years ago. Hand axe A lies in the sediment between X and Y. Hand axe B lies in the sediment below Y. Which conclusion is justified?
questions.skill: dating tools from the layers around them
questions.solution: **A was left between 1.4 and 0.9 million years ago, and B more than 1.4 million years ago.** Stone tools cannot be dated directly, so they are dated **from their environment**. In undisturbed layers, deeper layers are older. Axe A lies between two dated ash layers, so its age falls between their dates. Axe B lies below the older ash, so it is older than 1.4 million years, but nothing below it has been dated, so its maximum age is unknown. Nothing says A sits halfway between the ash layers or that sediment built up at a steady rate, so its age cannot be pinned to the mean of the two dates. B is not younger than A, because lower layers were laid down earlier. And the age of the stone itself is irrelevant: the rock formed long before anyone shaped it into a tool.

markScheme.description: A is between 1.4 and 0.9 million years old, and B is older than 1.4 million years

options: A is 1.15 million years old, the mean of the two ash dates, and B is 1.4 million years old
A was left between 1.4 and 0.9 million years ago, and B more than 1.4 million years ago
B is younger than A, because layers lower down were laid down more recently than higher ones
Both axes are over 1.4 million years old, because their stone formed before either ash layer

questions.prompt:
Scientists compared the base sequence of a gene found in all living organisms in three species: a bacterium, an archaean from a hot spring, and a human. Neither the bacterium nor the archaean has a nucleus in its cells. The table gives example figures.

| Pair compared | Bases identical (%) |
| --- | --- |
| archaean and human | 62 |
| archaean and bacterium | 51 |
| bacterium and human | 48 |

Which conclusion about classifying organisms without a nucleus do these data support?
questions.skill: why genetic analysis split the prokaryotes
questions.solution: **Organisms without a nucleus should not all be placed in one group.** The archaean's sequence is no closer to the bacterium's (51%) than to the human's (62%), so the two kinds of organism without a nucleus are not each other's closest relatives. Grouping all of them together, as the five kingdoms system did, hides a deep split, which is why genetic analysis led to the **three domains**: archaea and bacteria as two separate domains, and the eukaryota. Not having a nucleus is a shared feature, not evidence of close relationship. The archaean is not an animal: the domains group by deep ancestry, and a 62% match is far from the near-identical sequences of close relatives. And sequence data are used to classify precisely because each pair gives a different figure.

markScheme.description: organisms without a nucleus should not all be placed in one group

options: Archaea and bacteria belong in one kingdom, because neither has a nucleus
The archaean belongs in the animal kingdom, because it matches the human most closely
Sequence data cannot be used to classify, because every pair gives a different figure
Organisms without a nucleus should not all be placed in one group

questions.prompt: In the three domains classification system, one domain contains all the organisms whose cells have a nucleus, including animals, plants and fungi. Name this domain.
questions.solution: **Eukaryota** (the eukaryotes). The three domains are **archaea**, **bacteria** and **eukaryota**. Animals, plants, fungi and protists, which were four of the five kingdoms, all have cells with a nucleus and are placed together in the eukaryota. The organisms without a nucleus, once grouped as one kingdom of prokaryotes, were split into two domains, archaea and bacteria, after genetic analysis showed how different they are.

markScheme.description: eukaryota (eukaryotes)

questions.prompt: Ardi lived 4.4 million years ago and Lucy lived 3.2 million years ago. Assuming an average generation time of 20 years, calculate how many generations of human ancestors would fit into the time between Ardi and Lucy.
questions.solution:
Time between them: $4.4 - 3.2 = 1.2$ million years $= 1\,200\,000$ years.

Number of generations = time ÷ generation time $= 1\,200\,000 \div 20 = 60\,000$ generations.

Check: $60\,000 \times 20 = 1\,200\,000$. It is an estimate, because the dates are rounded and the generation time is assumed, but it shows why the fossils can record large changes: natural selection had tens of thousands of generations in which to act.

markScheme.description: finds the time between them, 1.2 million years (1 200 000 years), and divides by 20

questions.prompt: At a dig, a layer of volcanic ash is dated to 1.75 million years ago. Above the ash, sediment built up at a steady rate of 1.5 m every 100 000 years, and the layers have not been disturbed. A stone hand axe lies in the sediment 3 m above the top of the ash. Estimate how long ago the hand axe was left there, in millions of years.
questions.skill: dating a tool from a rate of deposition
questions.solution:
Time for 3 m of sediment to build up: $3 \div 1.5 = 2$ lots of 100 000 years $= 200\,000$ years $= 0.2$ million years.

The axe lies **above** the ash, so it is **younger** than the ash: $1.75 - 0.2 = 1.55$ million years ago.

Check: $1.55 + 0.2 = 1.75$. This is how a stone tool is dated **from its environment**: the stone itself cannot be dated, because the rock is far older than the tool. The estimate depends on the sediment really having built up at a steady rate, and on the axe not having been moved since it was buried.

markScheme.description: time for 3 m to build up: 3 ÷ 1.5 × 100 000 = 200 000 years (0.2 million years)
subtracts from the date of the ash, because the axe lies above it
1.55 million years ago

questions.prompt: Three fossil finds give evidence for human evolution: Ardi from 4.4 million years ago, Lucy from 3.2 million years ago, and the fossils discovered by Leakey from 1.6 million years ago. Describe how the features of these fossils change from the oldest to the youngest.
questions.solution: **Ardi** (4.4 million years ago) had feet suited to **climbing**, with a big toe that could grasp like a thumb, but other features suggest it could also **walk upright**. **Lucy** (3.2 million years ago) was more clearly adapted to **walking upright**: her knee and pelvis show a more human style of walking, though her **brain was still small** and her arms long. **Leakey's fossils** (1.6 million years ago) are more **human-like** again, with a **larger brain**, a shorter face and a body suited to walking and running long distances. Across the sequence the features become progressively more human, with upright walking developing first and the larger brain later.

markScheme.description: Ardi: feet suited to climbing with a grasping big toe, but some features of upright walking
Lucy: more clearly adapted to upright walking (knee and pelvis), but a small brain
Leakey's fossils: more human-like, with a larger brain, shorter face and a body suited to walking and running long distances

criteria.text: Describes Ardi with any two correct features (e.g. feet suited to climbing with a big toe that could grasp, features suggesting it could also walk upright, a small brain, long arms)
Describes Lucy with any two correct features (e.g. more clearly adapted to walking upright, with a knee and pelvis showing a more human style of walking; a brain that was still small; long arms)
Describes Leakey's fossils with any two correct features (e.g. a larger brain, a shorter face, a body suited to walking and running long distances, longer legs)

questions.modelAnswer: The oldest of the three, Ardi, from 4.4 million years ago, had feet suited to climbing trees, with a big toe that could grasp like a thumb. Other features of the skeleton, however, suggest that Ardi could also walk upright on two legs. Lucy, from 3.2 million years ago, was much more clearly adapted to walking upright: the structure of her knee and pelvis shows a more human style of walking. Her brain, though, was still small and her arms were long. The fossils discovered by Leakey, from 1.6 million years ago, are more human-like again. They show a larger brain, a shorter face, and a body suited to walking and running over long distances. Taken in order of age, the features become progressively more human, and in a particular order: upright walking developed first, and the brain became larger later.

questions.prompt: A newly discovered single-celled organism lives in a hot spring. Its cells have no nucleus, so under the five kingdoms system it would have been placed in the kingdom of prokaryotes. Explain why the lack of a nucleus cannot show which of the three domains the organism belongs to, and describe how genetic analysis would be used to decide.
questions.skill: placing a new organism in a domain
questions.solution: Organisms in **two** of the three domains, **bacteria** and **archaea**, have no nucleus, so this observable feature cannot tell them apart; it was by grouping such organisms on appearance that the five kingdoms system hid the difference between them. Scientists would **sequence** the organism's DNA (or RNA), for example a gene found in all living things, and **compare** it with the same sequence from known bacteria, archaea and eukaryotes. They would place the organism in the domain whose members' sequences are **most similar** to its own, because the more similar two sequences are, the more recently the organisms shared a **common ancestor**.

markScheme.description: both bacteria and archaea lack a nucleus, so the feature cannot tell the two domains apart
sequence its DNA or RNA and compare it with the same sequence in known bacteria, archaea and eukaryotes
place it in the domain with the most similar sequences, because more similar sequences mean a more recent common ancestor

criteria.text: Explains that organisms in two domains, bacteria and archaea, both lack a nucleus, so this feature cannot tell them apart
Describes sequencing the organism's DNA or RNA and comparing it with the same sequence from known members of the bacteria, archaea and eukaryota
Explains that it is placed in the domain whose sequences are most similar to its own, because more similar sequences mean a more recent common ancestor

questions.modelAnswer: Under the five kingdoms system, organisms were classified largely by their observable features, and every organism without a nucleus went into one kingdom, the prokaryotes. Genetic analysis later showed that this kingdom contained two groups so different from each other that each became a domain of its own: the bacteria and the archaea. Organisms in both of these domains lack a nucleus, so the absence of a nucleus tells scientists only that the new organism is not a eukaryote; it cannot show whether it is a bacterium or an archaean. To decide, scientists would sequence the organism's DNA or RNA, for example a gene that is found in every living thing, and compare the sequence of bases with the same gene in known bacteria, known archaea and known eukaryotes. The more similar two sequences are, the more recently the two organisms shared a common ancestor. The organism would be placed in the domain whose members' sequences are most similar to its own. Living in a hot spring is a clue, since many archaea live in extreme conditions, but it is the sequence comparison, not the habitat or the appearance, that settles the question.

questions.prompt: A human arm, a bat's wing and a whale's flipper are all pentadactyl limbs. Explain how natural selection could have produced these three different limbs from the limb of a common ancestor, and explain why their shared bone plan is evidence for evolution.
questions.skill: natural selection and the pentadactyl limb
questions.solution: The common ancestor had a **pentadactyl limb**: one bone in the upper part, two in the lower part, a group of small bones, then five digits. Its descendants **inherited** that plan. In each population there was **genetic variation** in the limb bones, such as their length and shape, arising from **mutation**. In each environment, the individuals whose limbs happened to suit their way of life better, such as longer digit bones supporting a wider wing in bats, or shorter, flatter bones forming a stiffer paddle in whales, were **more likely to survive and reproduce**, and they **passed on the alleles** for those features. Over many generations each limb was gradually modified in a different direction. Natural selection can only **modify what is already there**, so the same bones stayed in the same relative positions. If each species had arisen independently, there would be no reason for limbs used for grasping, flying and swimming to share one plan; the shared plan is best explained by **common ancestry**.

markScheme.description: Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): states that the limbs share a bone plan or that the best-suited individuals survive, with little linking of the steps

Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): explains part of the selection chain, such as variation and the survival of the best suited, or explains why a shared plan suggests a common ancestor, but not both, or leaves a gap such as no inheritance over generations

Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): explains the full chain: an ancestral plan inherited by all three, variation in the limb bones from mutation, the individuals whose limbs suited their way of life more likely to survive and reproduce, alleles passed on so each limb was modified over many generations, the same bones kept because selection modifies existing structures; and explains that limbs doing different jobs would not share a plan if the species had arisen independently

criteria.text: States that the common ancestor had a pentadactyl limb (one upper bone, two lower bones, small bones, five digits) and that its descendants inherited this plan
Explains that within each population there was genetic variation in the limb bones, such as their length and shape, arising from mutation

Explains that individuals whose limbs happened to suit their way of life better (e.g. longer digit bones in a bat's wing, shorter, flatter bones in a whale's flipper) were more likely to survive and reproduce
Explains that they passed on the alleles for these features, so over many generations each limb was gradually modified in a different direction
Explains that natural selection can only modify structures that already exist, so the same bones stay in the same relative positions
Explains that independent origins would not give limbs doing different jobs the same bone plan, so the shared plan is evidence of a common ancestor

questions.modelAnswer:
**The starting point.** The common ancestor of humans, bats and whales had a **pentadactyl limb**: one bone in the upper part, two bones in the lower part, a group of small bones, and five digits. Each group of its descendants **inherited** this limb plan.

**Variation.** Within each population the limb bones varied a little between individuals in length, thickness and shape. This **genetic variation** arose from **mutation**, and sexual reproduction mixed it into new combinations.

**Selection.** Different populations came to live in different ways. In the ancestors of bats, individuals whose digit bones happened to be longer could support a larger flap of skin and fly better, and were **more likely to survive and reproduce**. In the ancestors of whales, individuals with shorter, flatter arm bones forming a stiffer paddle swam better and were more likely to survive. They **passed on the alleles** for these features, so over many generations those features became more common, and each limb was gradually modified in its own direction.

**Why the plan survives.** Natural selection can only **modify what is already there**; every generation has to be able to survive, so it never starts again from scratch. That is why the same bones are still found in the same relative positions, differing in size and proportion.

**Why this is evidence.** If each species had arisen **independently**, there would be no reason for a limb used for grasping, one used for flying and one used for swimming to share a bone arrangement. The shared plan is best explained by **inheritance from a common ancestor**, followed by modification, which is evolution.

examTechnique.body:
Learn the three fossils **with their dates**, and present them as a **sequence** showing progressively more human features — **upright walking first, brains later**.

Say stone tools are dated **from their environment**, not directly. For the pentadactyl limb, the argument is **different jobs, same plan**, so inherited and modified.
examinerErrors: Naming the fossils without their dates.
Listing the fossils rather than showing a progression.
Omitting how stone tools are dated.
Saying the pentadactyl limb is evidence merely because limbs look similar.
Presenting the fossil record as complete.
Saying genetic analysis is "more accurate" without saying why appearance misled.
Calling the five kingdoms system careless or wrong.
Confusing the number of kingdoms with the number of domains.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 answer quotes the three fossils **with dates** and treats them as a **sequence** across 2.8 million years, noting that **upright walking comes before brain enlargement**. It remembers that stone tools are dated **from the layers around them**, because stone itself carries no date. On the pentadactyl limb it makes the real argument — **different jobs, one shared plan**, which independent origins would not predict — and draws out that evolution can only **modify what already exists**. It explains the domains change by the **weakness it fixed**: appearance can mislead, while **DNA and RNA** measure relatedness directly. And it treats the five kingdoms system as **good science superseded by better evidence**, not as a mistake.
